title: Your first project, from idea to live web address
intro: Here you'll walk the whole path once: you come up with something, tell the AI about it, it writes the page, you open it on your computer, ask for changes, and end up with an internet address you can send over WhatsApp. All of it is done by typing in the AI's text box and clicking buttons on three websites, without installing anything. By the end you'll have something of your own published, and you'll know how to repeat the process with any other idea.

theory.title: A webpage is a text file. That's it.
theory.text: What you see when you visit any website is a text file your browser knows how to read and paint on screen. That file is called HTML and could fit entirely on one sheet of paper. Inside it there's the text you read, instructions for colors and sizes, and the buttons that do things. You're not going to write it: you're going to ask the AI for it, and it hands it to you ready to copy and paste. Your job is deciding what has to go on it and checking that it turned out right.
theory.analogy: It's like a handwritten recipe. The paper isn't the food, it's the instructions. The browser is the cook who reads the recipe and serves you the dish.

theory.title: The full cycle: your computer, GitHub, Vercel
theory.text: Everything you're going to do follows the same route every time, and it helps to have it in mind before you start. First you work on your computer: you save the file and open it to look at it, and only you see it there, so you can get it wrong a thousand times without anyone knowing. When you like it, you upload it to GitHub, which is the closet where your project lives, saved and with history. As soon as it lands on GitHub, Vercel picks it up on its own and publishes it at an internet address that works for everyone. You change something, you upload it to GitHub again, and Vercel republishes without you asking. That loop is the whole craft.
theory.analogy: Your computer is your home kitchen, GitHub is the restaurant's fridge where you leave the finished dish, and Vercel is the waiter who carries it out to the dining room without you having to leave the kitchen.

theory.title: What this 'localhost' thing is
theory.text: Localhost literally means this computer, yours. It's the word used when the project is only being viewed on your own machine and no one else can get in. With a single-file page you don't even need to set anything up: you double-click and it opens in the browser, and at the top in the address bar you'll see it says file:// followed by your folder's path instead of an internet address. It means exactly the same thing: you're local, it's private, it's not published yet. On bigger projects the AI will tell you how to view them on localhost, but the idea doesn't change.
theory.analogy: It's the dress rehearsal with an empty house. Same stage, same set, but the theater doors are still closed.

theory.title: Two new accounts, zero dollars
theory.text: You're going to create two accounts and both are genuinely free, no card required: GitHub costs $0 for what you're going to do, and Vercel has a personal plan called Hobby that's also $0 and is plenty for publishing as many small pages as you want. You use the AI from whatever app you already have open, and this project works fine with the free version of ChatGPT, Claude, or Gemini; the paid ones run $20-25 a month and are for working longer stretches, not for this. The only thing that actually costs money is your own domain like mystore.com, about $10-15 a year, and that step isn't for today.

theory.title: How to ask the AI for things so they turn out right
theory.text: The AI doesn't guess, so give it context before you ask: who you are, what you know, what you want, and in what format. Always ask for the complete, full file, never the little piece that changed, because if it gives you a fragment you'll have to figure out where it fits, and that's where everyone gets stuck. Ask for one thing at a time: three small changes in a row work out better than one giant change. And when something breaks, describe it exactly as you see it, describing what's on your screen, without translating it into technical language.
theory.analogy: It's like commissioning furniture from a carpenter. If you say shelf, you get whatever he imagines. If you tell him which wall, what height, and what it needs to hold, you get yours.

theory.title: Something's going to break, and that's fine
theory.text: At some point the page will look wrong, a button will do nothing, or the file will open full of garbled characters. That's normal, it's not that you did something wrong. Nothing you do today can damage your computer or delete your files. The fix is almost always the same: paste what you're seeing to the AI and ask for the complete file again. And since every version you upload to GitHub is saved with its date, you can always go back to the previous one.

tasks.title: Write your idea in a single sentence
tasks.where: In a note on your phone or on paper
tasks.action: Before opening anything, write down what you want to make in a sentence that starts with 'a page that...' and says who it's for. Example: 'a page that shows my three physical therapy services and has a button to book via WhatsApp, for people in my neighborhood'. If three ideas come to mind, pick the smallest one: today's about finishing, not showing off.
tasks.expect: A single sentence written down, with a what and a who-for. If it doesn't fit in one sentence, the idea is still too big.
tasks.stuck: If nothing comes to mind, take the most boring thing you do every week and make a page for it: a menu, some hours, a price list, an introduction card about yourself.

tasks.title: Refine the idea by talking with the AI
tasks.where: In the ChatGPT, Claude, or Gemini app
tasks.action: Open a new conversation and paste the prompt below, swapping the bracketed part for your sentence. Answer its questions in plain, everyday language. Don't let it write the page yet.
tasks.prompt: I want to make a simple webpage and I don't know how to code at all, so talk to me without jargon. My idea is this: [PASTE YOUR SENTENCE HERE]. Before writing a single line, ask me five questions, one at a time, waiting for my answer before moving to the next, to understand what needs to appear on the page and who it's for. Once I've answered all five, summarize in ten lines what you're going to do and wait for me to say yes.
tasks.expect: The AI asks you one question, you wait, you answer, and so on five times. At the end it gives you a summary of what it's going to do and asks if you want to go ahead.
tasks.stuck: If it fires all five questions at once, answer them the same way in one numbered message. If it starts writing code without asking, tell it: 'stop, I don't want code yet, ask me the questions'.

tasks.title: Ask for the page as a single file
tasks.action: If the summary works for you, paste the prompt below. It's important to ask for a single file: that way there are no folders, no installations, no pieces that can get lost along the way.
tasks.prompt: The summary works, go ahead. I want the complete page in a single file called index.html, with the HTML, styles, and JavaScript all inside that same file. Nothing to install, no external libraries, and nothing that has to be downloaded separately. It should look good on mobile and on desktop. Give it to me as one single code block so I can copy it all at once, and below it, tell me in two sentences what you did.
tasks.expect: A long code block, starting with something like <!DOCTYPE html> and ending with </html>, with a copy button at the top right of the block.
tasks.stuck: If it gives you several blocks or talks about separate style files, reply: 'put it all into one single index.html file and give it to me again complete'.

tasks.title: Save the file on your computer
tasks.action: Click the copy button on the code block. Create a folder on your Desktop called my-first-website. Open Notepad (search for its name in the Start menu), paste inside with Ctrl+V, and go to File > Save As. There, under 'Type', choose 'All Files'; under 'Encoding', choose UTF-8; name it index.html and save it inside the my-first-website folder. On a Mac it's the same with TextEdit, but before pasting go to Format > Make Plain Text.
tasks.expect: Inside the my-first-website folder there's a file called index.html with your browser's icon (Chrome, Edge, or whichever you use), not Notepad's icon.
tasks.stuck: If the icon is still Notepad's, it got saved as index.html.txt because you didn't switch 'Type' to 'All Files'. Delete it and repeat Save As with that setting in place.

tasks.title: Open it and look at it on your computer
tasks.action: Double-click index.html. Your browser will open with the page. Look at the address bar at the top: it says file:// followed by your folder's path. That means you're viewing it locally, only you, and no one else can get in yet.
tasks.expect: Your page on screen, with your text, and at the top an address that starts with file:/// instead of https://. Even if it looks ugly, if you can see it, it already works.
tasks.stuck: If Notepad opens and you see the code text instead of the page, right-click the file > Open with > Chrome. If it opens blank, go back to the AI, tell it 'it opens blank', and ask for the complete file again.

tasks.title: Ask for three changes and look again
tasks.where: In the AI app and then on your computer
tasks.action: Looking at the screen, note three things you don't like and paste the prompt below with those three. When it gives you the new file, copy it, open your index.html with Notepad (right-click > Open with > Notepad), select all with Ctrl+A, paste over it with Ctrl+V, and save with Ctrl+S. Go back to the browser and press F5 to refresh.
tasks.prompt: I already have it open on my computer and I'm looking at it. I want three changes: 1) [first change]. 2) [second change]. 3) [third change]. Give me the complete index.html file again, whole, not just the piece that changes, and don't touch anything else that was already working.
tasks.expect: When you press F5 the page changes in front of you. This loop (ask, save, refresh) is the one you're going to repeat for the rest of your life.
tasks.stuck: If nothing changes when you refresh, press Ctrl+F5 to force the browser to forget the old version it had saved. If it still looks the same, check that you saved with Ctrl+S and that you're looking at the file in the my-first-website folder.

tasks.title: Create your GitHub account
tasks.action: Go to github.com and click 'Sign up' in the top right. It'll ask for an email, a password, and a username. Choose your username carefully: it's going to show up in your projects' addresses, so better your name or something sober than a nickname from fifteen years ago. Confirm the code that gets emailed to you. It costs $0 and doesn't ask for a card.
tasks.expect: You land on your GitHub page with your username in the top right and a message like 'Create your first repository'.
tasks.stuck: If it asks you to solve a puzzle to prove you're human, solve it yourself: it's part of signing up and no one can do it for you. If the confirmation email doesn't arrive, check the spam folder.

tasks.title: Upload your file to GitHub
tasks.action: Click the green 'New' button (or the + sign in the top right > 'New repository'). A repository is your project's folder saved on GitHub, with every previous version tracked. In 'Repository name' type my-first-website. Choose 'Private' if you'd rather the code not be visible to just anyone; the published page will look the same either way, this only hides the file's contents. Click 'Create repository'. On the next screen look for the 'uploading an existing file' link, drag your index.html into the area that appears, and scroll down to the green 'Commit changes' button. Every time you click that button, a snapshot of the whole project is saved with its date, and that snapshot is called a commit: it's the point you can return to if something breaks later on.
tasks.expect: The repository page with your index.html file in the list and, next to it, the upload time.
tasks.stuck: If you don't see the upload-files link, go into the repository and use 'Add file' > 'Upload files'. Warning: if you choose 'Public', anyone can view and copy the file from that moment on, and even if you later switch it to private, it may already have been copied; that can't be undone.

tasks.title: Create your Vercel account by signing in with GitHub
tasks.action: Go to vercel.com and click 'Sign Up'. Choose 'Continue with GitHub' and accept when GitHub asks if you authorize Vercel. When it asks what you'll use it for, choose the personal option, which is the Hobby plan: $0 and no card.
tasks.expect: The Vercel dashboard open, with your GitHub username at the top and an 'Add New...' button in view.
tasks.stuck: If the GitHub authorization window closes on its own, click 'Continue with GitHub' again. Authorizing Vercel gives it permission to read your repositories and publish them; you can revoke it anytime from GitHub, in Settings > Applications.

tasks.title: Publish the project
tasks.action: Click 'Add New...' > 'Project'. You'll see the list of your GitHub repositories. Find my-first-website and click 'Import' next to it. Don't change any of the settings that appear. Click the black 'Deploy' button (deploy: take your file and put it on the internet so anyone can see it) and wait thirty seconds to a minute.
tasks.expect: Either a congratulations screen with confetti and a thumbnail of your page, below it an address like my-first-website.vercel.app with a 'Visit' button.
tasks.stuck: If the deployment shows up red with 'Failed', open the log that appears, copy the error text, and paste it to the AI with this: 'this happens when I publish a single-file index.html page on Vercel, tell me what to do'.

tasks.title: Open your address and share it
tasks.where: In your browser and on your phone
tasks.action: Click 'Visit' and copy the address from the bar. Open it on your phone too, using mobile data, without your home wifi, to confirm it works from outside. Before sending it to anyone, read it through once: from that moment anyone with the link can see it, so remove anything from the page you don't want known (your exact address, your personal phone number, prices you're not sure about yet).
tasks.expect: Your page loading on your phone from an address ending in .vercel.app, without having had to install anything.
tasks.stuck: If it looks broken on mobile, go back to the AI with: 'on mobile it looks like this [describe it], fix it for small screens and give me the complete index.html again'.

tasks.title: Close the loop: change something and watch it republish itself
tasks.action: Ask the AI for a small, clearly visible change, like the title. Save the new file on your computer as before and check it with a double-click. Then go to your GitHub repository, click 'Add file' > 'Upload files', drag the new index.html over the old one, and click 'Commit changes'. Don't touch Vercel at all.
tasks.expect: Within a minute, refreshing your .vercel.app address with Ctrl+F5, the change shows up; and in the Vercel dashboard there's a new deployment moving from 'Building' to 'Ready'. That's the whole cycle: I work on my computer, I test it locally, I upload it to GitHub, it gets published on Vercel.
tasks.stuck: If the address still shows the old version, check the 'Deployments' tab in Vercel: if the latest one is 'Ready' and you still don't see it, it's your browser holding onto the old version; open it in an incognito window.

canDo: Publish a landing page, a menu, some hours, a portfolio, or a services page and have a real address to share today
Change text, colors, photos, and buttons as many times as you want without touching code: you ask the AI and it hands you the complete file back
Link your page to WhatsApp, an email, Google Maps, or your social profiles with a button
Repeat this exact process with any other idea, because the steps don't change even if the project does
Roll back to a previous version if you mess something up, because every upload to GitHub is saved with its date
cantDo: Actually charge money: taking card payments needs a payment gateway, and that's a different guide, not a button
Store data from your visitors (users, bookings, messages that stick around): a single-file page remembers nothing between visits
Have your own address like mybusiness.com without paying for the domain, which is separate and runs about $10-15 a year
Show up on Google on day one: publishing and ranking are different things, and the second one takes weeks
Build an application with user accounts and passwords: that needs pieces that don't fit in a single loose file
words: The text that every webpage is written in. Your browser reads it and paints it on screen. The AI writes it for you, in full.
The name of a website's main file. It's called that by convention: when someone visits your address, it's the one that opens by default.
This computer, yours. Said when you're the only one viewing the project, before publishing it. With a standalone file you recognize it because the address bar shows file:// instead of https://.
Your project's folder saved on GitHub, with every previous version tracked. A closet with memory.
Saving a change to GitHub with its date attached. Every time you click 'Commit changes' you create a point you can return to.
Taking your file and putting it on the internet so people can see it. It's what Vercel does automatically every time you upload something to GitHub.
A public repository can be read and copied by anyone; a private one only by you. The page published on Vercel looks the same either way: what changes is whether the file's contents are visible.
The address with your own name, like mystore.com. It's rented by the year, about $10-15 a year. The free address Vercel gives you ends in .vercel.app.
The copy your browser saves of a page to load it faster. It's the culprit when sometimes you don't see your change: fixed by pressing Ctrl+F5.
